Instructions

  1. There are 60 single-correct questions: Biology 1–15, Chemistry 16–30, Mathematics 31–45 and Physics 46–60.
  2. Each question has exactly one correct option. Correct: +4; incorrect: -1; unanswered: 0. All questions are available to attempt; there is no best-three-subject scoring rule.
  3. Use 180 minutes. An on-screen non-programmable scientific calculator is part of the 2026 examination conditions; personal calculators are not allowed under that scheme.
  4. Treat stated data and idealisations as exact unless an approximation is explicitly supplied. Log denotes base 10 and ln denotes the natural logarithm.
  5. The review PDF contains the question paper first, followed by a separate answer key and worked solutions. Keep the solutions hidden during a timed attempt.

Fixed authored order. Figures and IDs must remain linked during review.

Q1+4 / -1
A classification key lists P with jointed appendages and an exoskeleton, Q with a mantle and muscular foot, R with an adult water-vascular system and pentaradial body plan, and S with proboscis, collar and trunk. Which ordered assignment fits?
A) Annelida, Mollusca, Cnidaria, Chordata
B) Arthropoda, Annelida, Echinodermata, Chordata
C) Arthropoda, Mollusca, Cnidaria, Hemichordata
D) Arthropoda, Mollusca, Echinodermata, Hemichordata
Q2+4 / -1
The tissue diagram labels P as living elongated cells with uneven corner thickening, Q as dead heavily lignified fibres with narrow lumens, and R as a perforated conducting tube in a vascular bundle. A defect prevents normal lignification but leaves the corner-thickening process intact. Which prediction best distinguishes the tissue effects?
A) All three must become identical parenchyma immediately
B) P can retain collenchymatous support, while Q support and R's resistance to collapse are compromised
C) P loses all walls, while Q and R are unchanged because they are dead
D) R becomes phloem solely because its walls contain less lignin
Q3+4 / -1
Four meiotic events are recorded: homologous chromosomes pair, nonsister chromatids exchange corresponding segments, homologues separate while sister centromeres remain joined, and sister chromatids separate. Which ordering and interpretation are correct?
A) Synapsis precedes crossing over; homologues separate in division I and sisters in division II
B) Crossing over precedes synapsis; sister chromatids separate in division I
C) Homologues and sister chromatids always separate together in the first division
D) All four events are ordinary metaphase events of mitosis
Q4+4 / -1
In a C4 leaf, a four-carbon acid normally moves from mesophyll to bundle-sheath cells, releases CO2 there, and leaves a three-carbon compound that returns for acceptor regeneration. A selective block prevents this return while initially leaving decarboxylation and RuBisCO intact. Which early-to-later effect is most consistent?
A) Calvin-cycle reactions must all relocate into mesophyll cells
B) The initial four-carbon acid directly becomes RuBisCO and replaces its gene
C) Some existing acid can still release CO2, but sustained PEP regeneration and the concentrating shuttle decline
D) The block proves that C4 plants never use ATP for acceptor regeneration

B) Calcitonin deficiency is the stated cause, and PTH would lower calcium further
C) TSH directly supplies all missing calcium to the circulation
D) Loss of calcium-raising PTH fits the model; thyroid calcitonin has an opposing calcium-related action distinct from thyroxine

Which complete plan fits the stated stages and sites?

C) P culture then intrauterine transfer; Q transfer an already fertilised embryo as the unfertilised donor ovum; R ICSI

D) 2I0 and 2I0; constant π would interchange bright and dark positions rather than wash out contrast

A) n=2,Z=2,E=-13.6 eV

A) 1/2 and 1/2; neither past history fixes the order
B) 1/16 and 1/2; the older survivor must decay first
C) 1/2 and 1; the newly produced nucleus cannot decay during its first half-life

WORKED SOLUTIONS / B

Biology

Method, reasoning and common errors

Q1 Biology · easy

Diversity In the Living World / Diagnostic body structures distinguish five higher nonchordate groups without relying on names alone

Answer: (D) Arthropoda, Mollusca, Echinodermata and Hemichordata.

Why: Jointed appendages and an exoskeleton identify the arthropod combination. A mantle and muscular foot distinguish the molluscan plan. The water-vascular system, considered with adult pentaradial organisation, supports Echinodermata. The three-region body of proboscis, collar and trunk is characteristic of hemichordates; it must not be replaced by a chordate identity merely because of the historical name. Each assignment uses a distinctive structure rather than a general feature such as having a body cavity.

Why not the others: (A) exchanges arthropod and annelid characters and misassigns the last two groups. (B) gives a mantle-bearing animal an annelid identity and misclassifies S. (C) ignores the echinoderm water-vascular system.

Key point: Use diagnostic combinations to navigate a classification key.

Q2 Biology · medium

Structural Organisation In Plants And Animals / A selective wall defect separates collenchymatous support from lignified fibres and vessels

Answer: (B) Collenchyma and lignified support/conducting elements depend on different wall features.

Why: P's living cells and uneven corner thickening identify collenchyma, whose support does not depend on the same heavily lignified wall pattern as sclerenchymatous Q. R's perforated tube is a xylem vessel element arrangement; lignified walls help it withstand mechanical stresses and resist collapse during water transport. Being dead at maturity does not make Q and R independent of the wall properties established during differentiation. The specified defect therefore affects the tissues differently.

Why not the others: (A) assumes an immediate cell-identity conversion not caused by the stated defect. (C) destroys the explicitly preserved thickening mechanism and ignores lignified walls in dead mature cells. (D) treats loss of one wall component as automatic conversion between vascular tissues.

Key point: Link wall composition to function without replacing tissue identity.

Q3 Biology · medium

Cell: Structure And Functions / Meiotic pairing and exchange ordered separately from the two segregation events

Answer: (A) Pairing precedes crossing over, followed by the two different segregation events.

Why: Homologous pairing develops during zygotene, and crossing over between nonsister chromatids occurs during pachytene of prophase I. At anaphase I the homologous chromosomes move apart without the sister centromeres dividing in the ordinary meiotic pattern. Sister chromatids are separated during the second meiotic division. The chromosome relationships therefore differ at the two anaphases even though both move genetic material toward opposite poles.

Why not the others: (B) reverses the pairing/exchange sequence and assigns the wrong segregation event to division I. (C) eliminates the defining distinction between the two divisions. (D) assigns homologous synapsis and crossing over to ordinary mitosis.

Key point: Track homologues and sisters as different chromosome relationships.

Q4 Biology · medium

Plant Physiology / A blocked return intermediate distinguishes transient C4 decarboxylation from sustained acceptor regeneration

Answer: (C) Existing intermediates can support a transient step, but the carbon shuttle cannot be sustained.

Why: The initial carbon acceptor in the mesophyll is PEP. Its regeneration uses the returning three-carbon intermediate and requires energy. Existing four-carbon acid can initially reach a functioning decarboxylation step, so a transport block need not instantly poison RuBisCO or erase every intermediate. Over time, failure to return and regenerate the acceptor restricts continued operation of the concentrating pathway. The Calvin cycle remains associated with bundle-sheath CO2 fixation in the stated C4 arrangement.

Why not the others: (A) invents relocation of the Calvin cycle as an automatic response. (B) confuses a metabolic intermediate with a protein. (D) reverses the energetic requirement of PEP regeneration.

Key point: Separate a transient use of existing intermediates from a pathway's sustained regeneration requirement.

Q5 Biology · medium

Human Physiology / Preserved thyroxine feedback does not exclude loss of parathyroid calcium regulation

Answer: (D) PTH and calcitonin act in calcium regulation, whereas normal thyroxine does not replace PTH.

Why: Parathyroid hormone is a calcium-raising hormone, and its loss can account for the stipulated low-calcium effect in this model. Thyroid calcitonin has an opposing influence on blood calcium, but it is not the same substance as thyroid hormone involved in metabolic regulation. Normal thyroxine and its feedback therefore cannot be used as a test of intact parathyroid output. The question fixes the lesion and asks for hormonal interpretation rather than a unique diagnosis from symptoms alone.

Why not the others: (A) treats anatomically nearby endocrine sources as functionally identical. (B) reverses the calcium effect of PTH and changes the stipulated lesion. (C) assigns direct calcium supply to a pituitary signal.

Key point: Identify each hormone's source and regulated variable separately.

Q6 Biology · hard

Reproduction / Three stage-and-site constraints distinguish later embryo transfer, GIFT and ICSI

Answer: (A) Further culture with intrauterine transfer, GIFT and ICSI match the three constraints.

Step 1: Early embryos up to eight blastomeres can normally be transferred to the tube, but P's blocked tubes invalidate that route. Further culture permits transfer of a later embryo to the functional uterus.

Step 2: Q's aim is fertilisation within her body using a donor ovum. Gamete intrafallopian transfer provides the appropriate unfertilised gamete and patent-tube site.

Step 3: Direct sperm injection into the oocyte is intracytoplasmic sperm injection, a different operation from placing semen in the reproductive tract.

Why: Embryonic stage, anatomical access and whether fertilisation has already happened all constrain the route.

Why not the others: (B) ignores the tubal obstruction. (C) substitutes an embryo for the required unfertilised ovum. (D) confuses an intrauterine insemination site with the oocyte cytoplasm.

Key point: Match reproductive technology to stage, site and biological purpose.

Q7 Biology · medium

Genetics And Evolution / A deliberately mischarged adaptor separates amino-acid specificity from codon decoding

Answer: (B) Codon placement and amino-acid attachment are distinct specificity steps.

Why: The anticodon pairs antiparallel with the AAA codon, directing where this tRNA is used. The amino acid delivered is the molecule actually attached to the adaptor, here stipulated to be valine after editing has been bypassed. Normally aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase recognition and associated checks help maintain the correct amino-acid assignment. This experiment separates that charging specificity from the codon–anticodon interaction rather than changing the genetic code or the mRNA sequence.

Why not the others: (A) invents an RNA sequence mutation. (C) assigns amino-acid conversion to the ribosome without any such reaction. (D) ignores that different sites and recognition processes determine charging and decoding.

Key point: An adaptor's anticodon and its attached amino acid convey different information.

Q8 Biology · medium

Biology In Human Welfare / Dose-response adaptation separated from withdrawal and plant-source classification

Answer: (D) Tolerance, dependence and pharmacological class must be distinguished.

Why: Tolerance refers to reduced response to a previously effective dose, so the required dose may rise. Dependence is supported by a withdrawal syndrome after discontinuation in the stated history. These phenomena can coexist but are not interchangeable definitions. Drug source is another independent property: cocaine's plant origin does not make its stimulant action or molecular targets identical to opioid actions. The reports therefore describe different dimensions of drug use.

Why not the others: (A) confuses nervous-system adaptation with immunity to infection. (B) exchanges the two operational observations. (C) classifies receptor action from source alone and contradicts the stimulant description.

Key point: Classify the measured effect rather than treating every repeated-use change as dependence.

Q9 Biology · medium

Biotechnology / Transgenic protein production separated from resource-provenance and biopiracy concerns

Answer: (C) Technical production and the ethical provenance of resource use are different questions.

Why: Transgenic animals can be used to produce biologically useful human proteins; recovery and purification are then required to obtain a usable product. Biopiracy concerns unauthorised or unfair commercial use of biological resources and associated knowledge, as stipulated in the separate case. Demonstrating that a gene can be expressed does not establish the origin of the resource, consent or fair sharing. The question distinguishes biological application from the ethical issue rather than deciding the validity of a particular real patent.

Why not the others: (A) substitutes technical success for an assessment of provenance and permission. (B) misdefines a processing step as resource appropriation. (D) dismisses the very knowledge specified as part of the resource use.

Key point: Separate what a technology does from how its inputs and knowledge were obtained.

Q10 Biology · medium

Ecology / Four biodiversity-loss drivers identified by their distinct causal observations

Answer: (B) The four observations correspond to fragmentation, invasion, overexploitation and co-extinction.

Why: Dividing habitat reduces continuity and can isolate populations even where some habitat remains. An introduced predator adds an invasive biotic pressure. Excessive removal directly exceeds the harvested population's capacity to persist. In the final case, loss of an indispensable interacting species causes a dependent species to disappear, which is co-extinction. These drivers can interact in real ecosystems, but the observations specify the principal causal change for each case.

Why not the others: (A) exchanges the first two and last two mechanisms. (C) treats collection and introduction as though they were the same process. (D) attributes dependence-related loss to a case where habitat division is the specified cause and misassigns the other observations.

Key point: Identify the causal change, not only the shared outcome of population loss.

Q11 Biology · hard

Genetics And Evolution / Male-only gene flow separates adult allele pooling from sex-specific gamete contributions

Answer: (D) Adult pooled A frequency is 0.56, while offspring heterozygosity is 0.50.

Given: Migration is male-only and gametic contributions are equal within each sex, not across all adults regardless of sex.

Formula/Principle: Count adult alleles separately from the sperm and egg frequencies used to form offspring.

Step 1: Resident and immigrant A frequencies are pR​=0.40+0.20/2=0.50,pI​=0.64+0.32/2=0.80. Adult pooling gives padult​=500400(0.50)+100(0.80)​=0.56.

Step 2: Sperm frequency is ps​=300200(0.50)+100(0.80)​=0.60, while egg frequency remains pe=0.50.

Step 3: Heterozygotes arise from A sperm with a egg or a sperm with A egg. fAa​=ps​(1−pe​)+(1−ps​)pe​=0.60(0.50)+0.40(0.50)=0.50.

Why: Male-only immigration makes the two parental allele pools different. Applying 2p(1-p) to the pooled adult p would ignore the stated sex-specific gametic contributions. No founder bottleneck is required.

Why not the others: (A) ignores the immigrant effect on the adult allele count. (B) uses only immigrant frequencies. (C) treats the immigrant AA genotype frequency as an allele-pool quantity and applies the wrong mating model.

Key point: Construct the gamete pools actually used in mating before predicting offspring frequencies.

Q12 Biology · medium

Genetics And Evolution / Abiotic organic synthesis distinguished from demonstrated cellular life

Answer: (C) The result demonstrates a chemical-synthesis possibility within its specified conditions.

Why: The model tests whether supplied nonliving starting materials and an energy source can yield organic molecules. Detecting amino acids supports that stage of chemical evolution. A self-maintaining, reproducing cellular system would require additional organisation and processes that the observation explicitly does not establish. The result also depends on the chosen gas mixture and apparatus, so it cannot be transferred without qualification to every atmospheric composition.

Why not the others: (A) equates building blocks with an autonomous living system. (B) ignores the experimental conditions as part of the conclusion. (D) contradicts organic synthesis occurring with electrical discharges.

Key point: Match a claim about life's origin to the level of organisation actually produced.

Q13 Biology · easy

Human Physiology / Quiet breathing linked through diaphragm motion, thoracic volume and pressure gradient

Answer: (A) A changing alveolar–atmospheric pressure difference directs airflow.

Why: Expansion of the thorax and lungs lowers alveolar pressure slightly below atmospheric pressure, allowing air to enter. During ordinary quiet expiration, relaxation and elastic recoil reduce lung volume and raise alveolar pressure slightly above atmosphere, driving air out. The diaphragm's movement changes the volume; it does not directly pull individual air molecules through the airways. At the transition between phases pressures can equalise, but sustained flow requires a pressure gradient.

Why not the others: (B) reverses the inspiratory gradient and the normal diaphragm action in quiet expiration. (C) invents an extreme external pressure change. (D) eliminates the driving gradient while asserting flow.

Key point: Connect muscle action to volume, then pressure, then airflow.

Q14 Biology · medium

Cell: Structure And Functions / RNA sugar identity and phosphodiester polarity jointly locate the chain-extension site

Answer: (C) The structure is RNA, and normal chain extension uses the right-hand 3-prime OH.

Why: Ribose has the 2-prime hydroxyl shown, in contrast to deoxyribose's hydrogen at that position. Uracil provides a second compatible RNA feature. The backbone links a sugar's 3-prime position through phosphate to the next sugar's 5-prime position. A new nucleotide is therefore joined at the exposed 3-prime OH, extending the strand in the 5-prime-to-3-prime direction. Base amino groups do not provide the normal backbone extension site.

Why not the others: (A) contradicts the sugar and base evidence and extends the wrong end. (B) has the right nucleic-acid identity but an incorrect bonding site. (D) misidentifies the sugar and confuses the diagnostic 2-prime OH with the elongation 3-prime OH.

Key point: Use sugar composition to identify the strand and backbone polarity to locate its growth end.

Q15 Biology · medium

Biotechnology / Upstream oxygenation and downstream recovery separately limit scaled recombinant-product yield

Answer: (B) Upstream culture performance and downstream recovery can independently limit final yield.

Why: Product accumulated in a bioreactor depends on viable producing biomass and sustained physiological conditions, including adequate oxygenation for the stated culture. P's scale-up problem reduces that production capacity. Q instead loses material after production during processing, separation or purification. A per-cell expression measurement made in a small flask therefore omits both the number of productive cells over time and the fraction of their product recovered in usable form.

Why not the others: (A) treats gene presence as sufficient for the entire production process. (C) confuses physical recovery loss with a genetic change. (D) transfers a controlled small-scale measurement to different large-scale and processing conditions.

Key point: Distinguish expression, culture productivity and recoverable purified product.

WORKED SOLUTIONS / C

Chemistry

Method, reasoning and common errors

Q16 Chemistry · medium

Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure / Local hybridisation counts across alkene, alkyne, methylene and aldehyde centres

Answer: (A) Two sp, three sp2 and one sp3 carbon.

Step 1: Each of the two alkyne carbons has two electron-domain directions and is sp. Each of the two alkene carbons has three directions and is sp2.

Step 2: The aldehyde carbon also has three directions because its double-bonded oxygen counts as one direction, so it is sp2. The intervening CH2 has four sigma-bond directions and is sp3.

Why: Hybridisation is assigned locally; the presence of several multiple bonds does not make every carbon in the molecule the same type. Conjugation does not change the intervening saturated CH2 into a carbon with three bond directions.

Why not the others: (B) counts the carbonyl carbon as sp3. (C) counts only one of the two alkyne carbons as sp. (D) assigns an extra sp centre despite its three-direction bonding.

Key point: Count electron-domain directions separately at each carbon.

Q17 Chemistry · medium

Coordination compounds / Ligand-set exchange between complex cation and anion preserves oxidation states and total composition

Answer: (B) They are coordination isomers with complex-ion charges +3 and -3.

Step 1: A six-ammine M(III) ion has charge +3. A six-cyanido M(III) ion has charge +3−6=−3. Both written salts therefore balance electrically.

Step 2: The ligand sets are exchanged between two different metal centres in the complex cation and complex anion while the total composition is retained. This is coordination isomerism.

Why: Classifying the isomerism requires identifying what changes: the distribution of ligands between complex ions, rather than the donor atom of one ambidentate ligand or spatial arrangement within a fixed complex.

Why not the others: (A) invents a changed donor atom and miscounts ionic charges. (C) invokes a simple counterion exchange and a denticity change that do not occur. (D) changes neither metal's stated oxidation state and misidentifies the structural rearrangement.

Key point: Establish ionic composition before naming a coordination-isomer relationship.

Q18 Chemistry · hard

Structure of the Atom / An interior radial node and shell-volume factor distinguish 2s density from radial probability

Answer: (C) It is 2s, and the local probability density at the nucleus is nonzero.

Step 1: Spherical angular distribution identifies an s orbital, with l=0 and no angular nodes.

Step 2: The graph has one node at a positive radius. The radial origin is a boundary, not an additional nodal shell. Thus n−l−1=1 gives n=2.

Step 3: The given relation means local density is proportional to P(r)/r². Its specified positive limit therefore gives nonzero density at the nucleus.

Why: Radial probability includes the size of a spherical shell. That geometrical factor vanishes at zero radius even when the local density does not. The graph must be interpreted as the stated radial quantity, not as the wavefunction itself.

Why not the others: (A) omits the interior node and confuses the two probability quantities. (B) contradicts the spherical angular distribution. (D) counts a boundary as an extra radial node.

Key point: Distinguish radial probability, local density and an interior nodal shell.

Q19 Chemistry · medium

Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques / Two-step profile distinguishes local activation height from an absolute peak ordinate

Answer: (D) The larger local barrier is 70 kJ mol⁻¹ and the overall enthalpy is -20 kJ mol⁻¹.

Given: Each activation barrier is measured from the minimum immediately preceding its transition state.

Formula/Principle: Local barrier is transition-state energy minus its starting-state energy; overall enthalpy is final minus initial energy in this supplied profile.

Step 1: First-step barrier is 40−0=40 kJ mol⁻¹. Second-step barrier is 30−(−40)=70 kJmol−1.

Step 2: Overall change is −20−0=−20 kJmol−1.

Why: The lower absolute second peak still rises farther above its own deeper intermediate. Comparing peak heights alone does not compare local activation energies. This calculation does not by itself assert an overall rate-limiting step without population assumptions.

Why not the others: (A) reports the first barrier. (B) uses an absolute peak ordinate as a barrier. (C) reverses the sign of the reactant-to-product change.

Key point: Measure each barrier from its own preceding minimum.

Q20 Chemistry · easy

Hydrocarbons / Fused aromatic vertex counting separated from a single localised-bond picture

Answer: (B) The fused aromatic structure is C10H8 and is described by resonance.

Step 1: Two six-carbon rings share the two carbons on their common edge, giving 6+6−2=10 carbon atoms.

Step 2: The two shared junction carbons already bond to three other carbons and have no hydrogen. The remaining eight peripheral carbons each carry one hydrogen.

Why: A Kekulé-style alternating-bond sketch is a way of representing a conjugated aromatic system; it is not evidence that one fixed set of separate double bonds fully describes its electronic structure. Counting shared vertices also distinguishes fused rings from two rings linked by a single bond.

Why not the others: (A) ignores both fusion and unsaturation. (C) counts the two shared carbons twice and describes a different topology. (D) assigns hydrogens to the ring-junction carbons despite their valence.

Key point: Count the fused graph before adding hydrogens.

Q21 Chemistry · medium

Haloalkanes and haloarenes / Halogen deactivation and ortho/para direction describe different kinetic comparisons

Answer: (A) Overall reactivity and relative positional preference need not have the same trend.

Why: The halogen's electron-withdrawing inductive effect lowers the ring's overall susceptibility to electrophilic substitution. Its lone-pair interaction can nevertheless influence the relative stabilisation of intermediates for attack at different positions, favouring ortho and para relative to meta. Deactivation compares the substituted ring with benzene, whereas orientation compares competing positions within that substituted ring. These are different comparisons, so the stated combination is consistent.

Why not the others: (B) applies an exceptionless rule that fails for halogens. (C) treats one net kinetic observation as proof that a competing electronic effect is absent. (D) equates positional direction with overall activation.

Key point: Keep the reference comparison for rate distinct from the comparison among substitution sites.

Q22 Chemistry · medium

Alcohols, phenols, and ethers / A Williamson target has one suitable reagent orientation and one invalid aryl-SN2 reversal

Answer: (C) Phenoxide attacks the primary alkyl halide in P; Q is not the equivalent reversed route.

Why: Williamson synthesis requires a suitable substitution centre. Bromoethane offers a primary sp3 carbon at which phenoxide can displace bromide. Reversing the partners leaves bromine on an aromatic sp2 carbon; ordinary backside SN2 substitution at that aryl centre is not the corresponding viable process. Atom balance is necessary for a synthetic proposal but does not establish the required mechanism.

Why not the others: (A) ignores which atom bears the leaving group. (B) reverses the usual substrate suitability. (D) denies the nucleophilic role of alkoxide or phenoxide oxygen.

Key point: Choose which side supplies the nucleophile and which supplies the substitutable alkyl carbon.

Q23 Chemistry · medium

Aldehydes, ketones, and carboxylic acids / Carbonyl-carbon isotope retention resolves an otherwise ambiguous oxidative acid-fragment pair

Answer: (D) The isotope location, rather than the unlabelled acid pair alone, selects pentan-2-one.

Step 1: Pentan-2-one has a carbonyl carbon next to methyl and propyl groups. In the specified two-plus-three-carbon cleavage, retention with methyl gives labelled ethanoic acid.

Step 2: Pentan-3-one has an ethyl group on each side of its carbonyl. Retaining either side with that carbon gives a three-carbon labelled acid, propanoic acid.

Why: The supplied label tracks the original carbonyl carbon through a carbon-conserving cleavage. Without that tracking, the same pair of unlabelled fragment formulas would not distinguish the candidates under the stated conditions. No universal regioselectivity beyond the supplied cleavage model is assumed.

Why not the others: (A) gives pentan-3-one a methyl neighbour it does not possess. (B) ignores the conserved total of two plus three carbons. (C) discards the stated ambiguity that the isotope experiment resolves.

Key point: Track atom identity when product formulas alone are ambiguous.

Q24 Chemistry · medium

Organic compounds containing nitrogen / A temporary amino directing group establishes an alternating bromine pattern before reductive removal

Answer: (A) 1,3,5-Tribromobenzene.

Step 1: The amino group activates the original ortho and para positions, giving bromines at positions 2,4,6 relative to the original NH2 carbon.

Step 2: Cold diazotisation converts NH2 to the diazonium group. H3PO2 replaces that group by H rather than by OH or CN. The three bromine positions are unchanged.

Step 3: Without the original amino substituent, renumbering from a brominated carbon gives the alternating pattern 1,3,5.

Why: A temporary directing group can establish a substitution pattern and then be removed; replacing the group does not move the other substituents.

Why not the others: (B) stops before diazotisation and deamination. (C) uses the hydrolysis product associated with water rather than the supplied reducing reagent. (D) removes two bromines without a stipulated reaction.

Key point: Preserve ring connectivity while renumbering after removal of a directing group.

Q25 Chemistry · easy

Solutions / A second nonvolatile solute changes the full solvent mole-fraction denominator

Answer: (B) The ratio is 0.80 because both nonvolatile solutes contribute particles.

Given: Solvent amount is 1.00 mol and total solute amount is 0.25 mol.

Formula/Principle: For an ideal solution with nonvolatile solutes, psolvent​=xsolvent​p0.

Step 1: xsolvent​=1.00/(1.00+0.10+0.15)=1/1.25=0.80.

Step 2: The ratio 1/1.10 would omit Y from the denominator even though it is another dissolved particle population.

Why: Raoult's law uses mole fraction in the entire liquid mixture, not a separately normalised solvent–X subsystem.

Why not the others: (A) neglects Y and also approximates the remaining ratio incorrectly. (C) subtracts amounts without dividing by total moles. (D) inverts the mole-fraction ratio.

Key point: Include every dissolved species in the mole-fraction denominator.

Q26 Chemistry · medium

Electrochemistry / Electron-weighted Gibbs-energy addition combines unequal-electron reduction steps

Answer: (C) The combined potential is +0.10 V and ΔG°=-0.30F.

Given: The two reductions have different electron counts and sum to the target reaction.

Formula/Principle: Gibbs energies are additive; potentials themselves are not extensive.

Step 1: ΔG1∘​=−F(0.50),ΔG2∘​=−2F(−0.10)=+0.20F.

Step 2: ΔGsum∘​=−0.30F.

Step 3: The total electron count is three, so E∘=−ΔGsum∘​/(3F)=0.10 V.

Why: Electron weighting enters through the energy relation before converting back to the intensive potential.

Why not the others: (A) directly adds potentials. (B) takes an unweighted arithmetic mean. (D) reverses the sign of the final reduction.

Key point: Add energies for combined electrochemical reactions, then divide by the total electron count.

Q27 Chemistry · medium

Chemical Kinetics / Excess-reactant control changes the observed order and slope without changing the intrinsic law

Answer: (D) Excess B produces a pseudo-first-order observation without changing the intrinsic two-reactant law.

Step 1: With B effectively constant in each run, r=(k[B])[A]=kobs​[A].

Step 2: Integration gives ln[A]=ln[A]0​−kobs​t. Thus ln[A] is linear in time.

Step 3: kobs,Q​/kobs,P​=0.40/0.20=2.

Why: The controlled concentration becomes part of the observed coefficient. A first-order trace in one monitored reactant is not proof that the intrinsic law contains only that reactant.

Why not the others: (A) ignores the excess-reactant approximation. (B) confuses constant intrinsic k with the concentration-dependent observed coefficient. (C) assigns an order from amount alone.

Key point: Distinguish an intrinsic rate constant from a pseudo-order coefficient.

Q28 Chemistry · medium

Thermodynamics / A matched dilution blank changes the inferred weak-acid ionisation enthalpy

Answer: (A) HA ionisation is endothermic by 7.0 kJ mol⁻¹.

Given: Positive quoted heats mean energy released; the blank is a nonreaction contribution.

Formula/Principle: Hess's law compares the weak-acid reaction with the strong-ion neutralisation after subtracting the blank.

Step 1: Weak-acid reaction heat release alone is 5.20−0.20=5.00 kJ. Its molar reaction enthalpy is -50.0 kJ mol⁻¹; the strong-acid value is -57.0 kJ mol⁻¹.

Step 2: Dissociation followed by proton neutralisation gives the weak-acid reaction. ΔHion​+(−57.0)=−50.0 ⇒ ΔHion​=+7.0 kJmol−1.

Why: Ionisation absorbs some of the heat released in the common proton–hydroxide step. A dilution background must not be assigned to that ionisation.

Why not the others: (B) omits the dilution correction. (C) reverses the enthalpy sign. (D) fails to convert the 0.100 mol heat difference to a per-mole value.

Key point: Correct measured heat contributions before using a Hess comparison.

Q29 Chemistry · medium

Equilibrium / Solid-phase exhaustion limits equilibrium gas pressure in one of two otherwise identical vessels

Answer: (B) P reaches 0.40 bar while Q exhausts carbonate at 0.10 bar.

Given: Each mole CO2 raises pressure by 1.00 bar in either vessel.

Formula/Principle: The Kp pressure condition for the displayed heterogeneous equilibrium requires both solid phases to remain available.

Step 1: Reaching 0.40 bar requires decomposition of 0.40 mol carbonate. P has enough, leaving 0.60 mol and retaining both solids.

Step 2: Q can release only 0.10 mol CO2 before its carbonate disappears. pQ​=(0.10 mol)(1.00 barmol−1)=0.10 bar.

Why: Once a required solid phase is absent, blindly setting the gas pressure to Kp would demand more reactant than exists. The phase-exhausted boundary must satisfy the material inventory.

Why not the others: (A) ignores Q's limiting carbonate amount. (C) equates all P carbonate with obligatory decomposition despite equilibrium. (D) reverses the inventories.

Key point: Check phase availability before imposing a heterogeneous equilibrium expression.

Q30 Chemistry · hard

The d- & f-block elements / Formal f-electron accounting linked to lanthanoid exceptions and actinoid oxidation-state variation

Answer: (C) The formal counts are 4f0, 4f7 and 5f0, with electron energetics rather than atomic mass as the relevant explanation.

Step 1: Ce loses its two 6s, one 5d and one 4f valence electrons to reach Ce4+, leaving 4f0.

Step 2: Eu loses its two 6s electrons to form Eu2+, preserving the half-filled 4f7 arrangement.

Step 3: U6+ formally loses the six electrons distributed over 7s,6d and5f, leaving 5f0.

Why: The dominant +3 tendency of lanthanoids does not prohibit particular +2 or +4 states. Empty or half-filled configurations contribute to some exceptions, while participation of nearby-energy actinoid orbitals allows a wider range of oxidation states. This is not a prediction that every formally writable ion is equally stable in every medium.

Why not the others: (A) stops removing electrons despite the required charges. (B) has the counts but replaces orbital energetics with an unsupported mass rule. (D) gives cations extra electrons instead of removing them.

Key point: Reconcile charge with the whole valence configuration before explaining f-block exceptions.

Q31 Mathematics · medium

Matrices & determinants / Concrete matrix identity reduces a high-degree polynomial to a linear matrix expression

Answer: (B) -1.

Given: The concrete product identity can reduce every higher power.

Formula/Principle: Multiply the identity by powers of A and combine like matrix terms before taking a determinant.

Step 1: A3=3A2−2A=7A−6I, and A5−3A4=A3(A2−3A)=−2A3.

Step 2: Hence the matrix inside the determinant is −2(7A−6I)+4(3A−2I)−I=3I−2A.

Worked derivation: 3I−2A=(34​−2−3​),det=−9+8=−1.

Why: Matrix multiplication distributes over these polynomials in the same matrix. Reducing the polynomial is shorter and less error-prone than expanding fifth powers entry by entry.

Why not the others: (A) loses the determinant sign. (C) uses only one diagonal entry. (D) confuses a scalar multiple or trace with the determinant.

Key point: Reduce the matrix polynomial before evaluating its determinant.

Q32 Mathematics · easy

Permutations and Combinations / Repeated intact blocks and disjoint endpoint cases in a multiset arrangement

Answer: (D) 12.

Given: The two AB tiles are indistinguishable from each other, as are the two C tiles.

Formula/Principle: Count the endpoint cases and divide by factorials for repeated units.

Step 1: Fix D at the left end. The four remaining tiles can be arranged in 4!/(2!2!)=6 distinct ways.

Step 2: D at the right end gives another six. Since there is only one D tile, these two cases cannot overlap.

Worked derivation: N=6+6=12.

Why: AB is one indivisible tile, not two letters whose positions may be separated. Identical-tile permutations do not make different rows.

Why not the others: (A) counts only one end. (B) divides by only one repeated-pair factorial after selecting the endpoint. (C) counts unrestricted positions of D.

Key point: Identify the true repeated units before imposing an endpoint condition.

Q33 Mathematics · medium

Relations & functions / An onto composition constrains the final factor but leaves an unused intermediate element

Answer: (A) Twelve maps work; g is necessarily onto but f is not onto its four-element codomain.

Formula/Principle: An onto composition must attain both final outputs on the image of f.

Step 1: Of the eight assignments of g on a,b,c, exclude the two constant assignments. Six assignments remain.

Step 2: g(d) can independently be 0 or 1. Thus N=(23−2)2=12.

Worked derivation: Both outputs already occur among g(a),g(b),g(c), so g is onto; f still never reaches d.

Why: Surjectivity of the composition forces the last map to cover its codomain, but does not require the first map to use every intermediate element.

Why not the others: (B) reverses the necessary implication. (C) subtracts too few constant-on-image assignments and misstates f's property. (D) omits the choice at d and contradicts g's forced surjectivity.

Key point: Distinguish the intermediate codomain from the actual image used by the composition.

Q34 Mathematics · medium

Step 2: (1+2i)2=−3+4i,(1−2i)2=−3−4i.

Key point: Do not replace complex squares by squared magnitudes.

Q35 Mathematics · hard

Integration / A minimum of two curves and an absolute value require two different sets of breakpoints

Answer: (D) 16(√2-1)/3.

Given: The minimum can change formula, and its selected formula can also change sign.

Formula/Principle: Locate crossings before applying the absolute value; exploit even symmetry only after identifying the pieces.

Step 2: Therefore I=2[∫01​x2dx+∫12​​(2−x2)dx+∫2​2​(x2−2)dx].

Step 3: The three positive-half contributions are 1/3,(42​−5)/3,(42​−4)/3.

Why not the others: (A) evaluates the signed integral without the absolute value. (B) counts only the positive half-axis. (C) loses the constant endpoint contributions.

Q36 Mathematics · medium

Three-dimensional geometry / A direction parameter gives parallelism while an independent base-point parameter gives coincidence

Answer: (B) k=4 and b=2.

Step 1: The x and z components force the second direction to be twice the first. Its y component must then be 4, so k=4.

Step 2: The base-point displacement is (b-1,2,-1). It must equal λ(1,2,-1). The y and z components give λ=1 and therefore b=2.

Worked derivation: (2,2,1)=(1,0,2)+(1,2,−1), so L2 starts on L1 and has the same direction.

Why not the others: (A) gives parallel but displaced lines. (C) fails the direction ratio. (D) gives an inconsistent y-direction sign.

Key point: Test direction and position separately.

Q37 Mathematics · easy

Step 1: y2=x4 ⇒ y=x2ory=−x2.

Why not the others: (B) interprets division by zero as an infinite slope without checking the numerator. (C) assigns slopes not obtained from either branch. (D) contradicts direct substitution.

Key point: Resolve branches when a formal implicit derivative becomes indeterminate.

Q38 Mathematics · medium

Statistics / Pairing observations with affine reflections changes a pooled variance through mean separation

Answer: (C) Mean 4 and population variance 7.

Given: Each original observation contributes a pair x,8-x.

Formula/Principle: Compute paired deviations about the new mean, including the separation of the two group means.

Step 1: Each pair sums to 8, so the new mean is 4.

Step 2: Each pair's deviations from 4 are x-4 and its negative. Thus new variance is E[(x−4)2] over the old set.

Worked derivation: E[(x−4)2]=E[(x−2)2]−4E[x−2]+4=3+0+4=7.

Why: Reflection preserves within-group variance, but merging groups with means 2 and 6 adds a between-group contribution. Simply duplicating the original set would not do that.

Why not the others: (A) omits group separation. (B) treats reflection as unchanged duplication. (D) uses only the reflected group's mean.

Key point: Account for both within-group dispersion and different group centres.

Q39 Mathematics · medium

Limit & continuity / A floor-function squeeze controls a trigonometric quotient at infinity

Answer: (D) 1.

Q46 Physics · medium

Q47 Physics · medium

Q48 Physics · medium

Work, Energy and Power / Closed-path work fixes total dissipation but only bounds an individual potential difference

Worked derivation: ⟨I⟩=21​(4I0​+0)=2I0​ at both selected positions.

Why: Loss of stable relative phase during averaging reduces contrast; a fixed phase change retains coherence and moves maxima.

Why not the others: (A) omits switching and misstates a fixed-phase effect. (B) describes one phase state rather than the average. (C) violates the summed background intensity and invents a wavelength change.

Key point: Distinguish a stable phase shift from a fluctuating phase that averages away interference.

Q59 Physics · hard

Atoms / Orbit circumference and matter wavelength jointly determine ionic charge and level energy

Answer: (D) n=4,Z=8 and energy -54.4 eV.

Given: The wavelength is a matter wavelength around the orbit, not an emitted photon's wavelength.

Formula/Principle: Apply the orbit standing-wave condition before the radius and energy relations.

Step 1: n=2πr/λ=2π(2a0​)/(πa0​)=4.

Step 2: 2a0​=a0​(16/Z) ⇒ Z=8.

Step 3: E=−13.6(82/42)=−54.4 eV.

Worked derivation: The circumference contains four wavelengths, and n2/Z=2 reproduces the supplied radius.

Why: Radius alone fixes only a ratio of quantum numbers; the independent matter-wave condition separates them.

Why not the others: (A) violates the circumference count. (B) uses the right n but fails the radius. (C) doubles n despite the measured wavelength.

Key point: Use independent quantisation constraints before evaluating the energy.

Q60 Physics · medium

Nuclei / Conditional survival distinguishes a statistical half-life from an individual nuclear lifetime

Answer: (A) Both next-interval survival probabilities are 1/2; their actual decay order is not fixed.

Given: For a nucleus present at time zero, survival to t has probability S(t)=exp(-λt), and λT=ln 2.

Formula/Principle: Condition on the fact that the older nucleus is still present; do not count its earlier survival twice.

Step 1: For the older survivor, P(survive to 4T∣survived to 3T)=S(3T)S(4T)​=2−32−4​=21​.

Step 2: The newly produced nucleus survives its next T with probability S(T)=e−λT=21​.

Worked derivation: More generally, S(t)S(t+T)​=e−λT=21​, independent of its elapsed survival time t.

Why: A constant decay constant gives the same future decay probability per unit time to each nucleus that remains. Half-life characterises an ensemble probability, not a scheduled maximum life or an ageing countdown for an individual nucleus. Equal probabilities do not predict the realised decay order of these two nuclei.

Why not the others: (B) uses the unconditional probability of surviving all four half-lives instead of conditioning on the first three already survived. (C) invents an initial interval during which decay is impossible. (D) treats three half-lives as an individual lifetime limit despite the nonzero exponential survival probability.

Key point: Reset the probability calculation at the observation time for nuclei known to have survived.
